newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Khmer Rouge hardliners said to defect.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rouge hardliners said to defect.

text.p: About 150 Khmer Rouge members defected to the Cambodian government on Monday and negotiators tried to persuade feared commander Ta Mok to follow suit, military officials said.
"One hundred and fifty Khmer Rouge hardliners decided to join the government today," said General Nuon Vana, deputy to northwest regional military commander General Khan Savoeun.
Nuon Vana said Khan Savouen had flown to the defectors' village at Sre Phrang, about 30 km (18 miles) southeast of the Khmer Rouge base at Anlong Veng, close to the border with Thailand.
He did not know how many of the 150 defectors were guerrillas and how many were their dependants.
The Khmer Rouge, whose 1975-79 rule left at least one million people dead, reneged on a 1991 peace pact and had been fighting the coalition government since 1993.
The movement began crumbling after former top official Ieng Sary split with hardliners in August.
Thousands of guerrillas have come over to the government side, but an estimated 2,000 hardliners loyal to Khmer Rouge leaders Pol Pot and Ta Mok are holding out around Anlong Veng.

Nuon Vana said 15 negotiators and pilots, who had been missing since Friday, were in Anlong Veng and negotiating with the one-legged commander Ta Mok, known as "The Butcher" for his ruthless reputation.
"They are there to carry on negotiations in order to persuade more Khmer Rouge" to join the coalition government, he said.
The defection of Ta Mok, viewed along with Pol Pot as the most hardline leader, would probably prove fatal to the Maoist group as a guerrilla movement, analysts said.
It was not clear if the helicopter pilots and negotiators were being forced to stay in Khmer Rouge territory against their will.
Military officials had said on Sunday that the group was being held hostage after Ta Mok lured them by saying he wanted to defect.
The negotiators at Anlong Veng are members of the royalist FUNCINPEC party.
FUNCINPEC and the Cambodian People's Party (CPP), which formed an uneasy coalition government after U.N.-run polls in 1993, have been vying for the allegiance of Khmer Rouge defectors.
